lesson.text: Quick memory: what is a search engine's index? (A giant list of words and the pages they are on.) Today: why some results come first.
A search engine sends out programs called crawlers. They visit pages and follow their links, again and again, adding every page's words to the index.
When you search, the search engine finds every page with your words, then ranks them: it puts them in order, with the pages it thinks will help you most at the top.
It ranks by clues. Is every search word on the page, even in its title? Do many other pages link to it, like friends recommending it? Is it new? Is it in your language?
Worked example: two pages both have all your words. 30 pages link to page A and only 5 to page B, so page A usually ranks higher: more pages point to it.
Adverts: companies pay to put their pages at the top, marked Ad or Sponsored. An advert is there because someone paid, not because it is the best answer.
The top result is not always true or the best. Check it the grade 4 way: who wrote it, when and why? Then compare it with another good page.
Try it in the world: with a grown-up, search for the same question in two different ways. Which results moved up or down, and which were adverts? Next: real or edited pictures.

exercises.prompt: What does a search engine's crawler do?
exercises.hint: Think of a spider walking along the web's threads.
choices: visits pages and follows their links
exercises.explain: A crawler visits pages, follows their links to more pages, and adds their words to the index.

exercises.prompt: Adverts in search results are marked with words like Ad or Sponsored.
exercises.hint: Look at the first result in the picture.
exercises.explain: True: adverts are marked, so you can tell them from other results.

exercises.hint: Look for the small tag in front of a result.
exercises.explain: The first result has the Ad tag: someone paid to put it there.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: is it a clue a search engine ranks by, or not?
items: your words in the page's title
exercises.hint: Would it help the search engine guess which page answers you best?
exercises.explain: Your words, links and how new a page is are clues. A background colour or a favourite food don't help.

exercises.prompt: This search engine puts pages with more of your search words first; if two tie, the one with more links comes first. Put the pages in order.
exercises.hint: Sort by search words first. Only when two pages tie, look at the links.
exercises.explain: Buzz Facts (4 words, 20 links) and Honey Farm (4 words, 12 links) tie on words, and Buzz Facts has more links. Bee Club has only 2 words.

exercises.prompt: Why is an advert at the top of the results?
exercises.hint: What does the Ad tag tell you?
choices: Someone paid for it to be there
exercises.explain: An advert is at the top because someone paid for it to be shown there.

exercises.prompt: The first result is always the most correct answer.
exercises.hint: Is ranking the same as checking that something is true?
exercises.explain: False: ranking is the search engine's best guess from clues. Check the page yourself.

exercises.prompt: Mimi and Juno search the same words in different countries. Why may their results differ?
exercises.hint: Think of the clues a search engine uses.
choices: Search engines use where you are as a clue
One of them typed it wrong
exercises.explain: Where you are and your language are clues, so people in different places can see different results.

exercises.prompt: Match each part to what it does.
exercises.hint: Think about how a search engine finds, lists and orders pages.
exercises.explain: The crawler visits pages, the index lists their words, ranking orders the results, and adverts are paid for.

exercises.prompt: A page repeats the word dragon 500 times but says nothing useful. Why might a good search engine rank it low?
exercises.hint: Is having the word lots of times the only clue?
choices: It uses other clues too, like links to it
exercises.explain: Search engines use many clues. Few good pages link to a useless page, so it ranks low.

exercises.prompt: This search engine puts pages with more search words first; if two tie, more links wins. Put them in order.
exercises.hint: Search words first, biggest first. Break each tie with the links.
exercises.explain: Nature Notes and Garden Tips have 3 words (18 and 9 links), then Meadow News and Bee Club have 2 (25 and 7 links).

exercises.prompt: Sort these results: an advert, or a result that earned its place?
items: Ad · Toy Shop: dragons half price
exercises.hint: Look for the words Ad and Sponsored.
exercises.explain: The Ad and Sponsored results are paid for. The others earned their places by the search engine's clues.

exercises.prompt: What is the best way to check a top result?
exercises.hint: Being first is not the same as being true.
choices: Compare it with another trusted page
Believe it because it is first
Click the advert next to it
Search until you find what you hoped
exercises.explain: Compare it with another trusted page, and ask who wrote it, when and why.

exercises.prompt: More links pointing to a page is a bit like more people recommending it.
exercises.hint: Why would many pages link to one page?
exercises.explain: True: pages link to pages they think are useful, like recommendations, so links are a ranking clue.
